newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany indicts Compuserve on Internet porn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany indicts Compuserve on Internet porn.

text.p: German prosecutors stepped up their war against Internet smut on Wednesday, pressing charges against a local Compuserve manager in what could be a test case to see how far authorities can go in policing cyberspace.

After over a year of official investigations, Bavarian prosecutors have indicted the head of the German unit of U.S. online service Compuserve Corp in connection with the distribution of pornography and Nazi writings over the Internet.

The charges date back to an investigation begun at the end of 1995, when Bavarian authorities sparked an outcry among cyber-liberty advocates by forcing Compuserve to close down access to over 200 sex-related Internet news groups.

While the prosecutors did not name the accused in their press release, Compuserve officials confirmed the charges were filed against Felix Somm, mangaing director of Compuserve operations in Germany and Central Europe.

"He is accused in numerous instances in 1995 and 1996 of knowingly allowing images of child pornography, violent sex and sex with animals from newsgroups from the so-called Internet to be accessible to customers of Compuserve Germany," Munich prosecutors said in the statement.

The prosecutors also said that certain computer games available to Compuserve members in Germany violated laws against "glorifying violence" and contained outlawed pictures of Adolf Hitler and Nazi symbols such as swastikas.

The specific charges against Somm are "assisting in the distribution of pornographic materials as well as premeditated and negligent violation of laws concerning writings that are dangerous to youths," the statement said.
Compuserve's German unit declined commment, saying it would issue a statement later in the day.
The prosecutors' office was not immediately available for comment.

The indictment, issued on February 26 but not made public until Wednesday, is the first of its kind in Germany and is bound to spark renewed debate about how far the long arm of the law can reach into cyberspace.

Despite a raging dispute over the liability of online services for what users do over their networks, German prosecutors believe such services are reposonible when writings or images outlawed in Germany but on computers somewhere else in the world are made accessible to Germans over the Internet.

Internet service providers such as EUnet Deutschland GmbH or online services Compuserve and America Online have argued that so-called filtering software that allows parents to control what children see online is protection enough.

But prosecutors have been frustrated in their efforts to break child pornography and prostitution rings that use the Internet to reach their customers or neo-Nazis who use it to spread hate diatribes that would be outlawed in Germany.

Bonn's draft multimedia law makes an effort to protect internet service providers against undo prosecution, but appears to leave a loop-hole that would allow police to make providers and online service responsible in the end.

"The multimedia law states that a provider must use reasonable technical measures to control the content on their networks," said Harald Summa, head of the Internet Media Council, a lobby group for Internet service providers.
It appears that the Munich prosecutors want to set a precedent and prove that Somm did not do what was technically possible to stop the transmission of cybersmut to Germans.
"He could have put a computer in operation that was able to block certain newsgroups," the prosecutors" statement said.
